What does it depend on?

What should we count?

::: notes
Blanks are for the pen. What the room should land on:

- the **size** of the array
- **where q is** -- or whether it is there at all
- the **speed of the machine**

The third one is the one to kill: we are not benchmarking, so machine speed
has to go. That is what forces us to count operations instead of seconds --
and the first two are what force us into cases.
:::

## Best, worst, average {.smaller}

```cpp
int idxFirst (vector<int> arr, int q) {
    for (int i = 0; i < arr.size(); i++)
        if (arr[i] == q)
            return i;
    return -1;
}
```

For an array of size $n$:

- best case &nbsp; $T(n) =$
- worst case &nbsp; $T(n) =$
- average case &nbsp; $T(n) =$

::: notes
Best: 1 -- q is at index 0. Worst: n -- q is last, or absent. Average: about
n/2, and it is worth asking *average over what?* -- you have to assume a
distribution before "average" means anything. That assumption is where most
average-case analysis quietly goes wrong.

Which of the three do we usually report, and why? Worst case: it is a promise
you can actually make.
:::

{{< countdown minutes=3 >}}

::: notes
The point of this one: **there is no early return.** Best and worst are the
same -- $n-1$ comparisons either way. The loop has to see every element to
know it has the minimum.

That is the contrast with `idxFirst`, where the cases genuinely differ. Some
algorithms have cases; some don't. Worth saying out loud.

The array is rigged so the minimum is at index 0 -- students who are pattern
matching on `idxFirst` will call that the best case. It isn't.
:::

## Examining the details {.smaller}

```cpp
int idxFirst (vector<int> arr, int q) {
    for (int i = 0; i < arr.size(); i++)
        if (arr[i] == q)
            return i;
    return -1;
}
```

How many lines are executed in the worst case?

$$T(n) = $$

::: notes
Count it with them, line by line, with the pen. A defensible answer is
$T(n) = 2n + 2$ -- the loop test and the comparison each run about n times,
plus the initialisation and the final return.

Do not fight about the exact constant. Getting two different numbers from two
students is the *setup* for the next question, not a problem.
:::

## Does it matter? {.smaller}

$$T(n) = 2n + 2$$

\

Does the **2n** matter?

Does the **+2** matter?

::: notes
This is the hinge into asymptotics, and it is worth slowing down for.

The +2 is gone the moment n is large. The coefficient 2 survives scaling but
not a change of machine -- a computer twice as fast erases it. What no machine
erases is the **n**.

Land it: the only durable thing about $2n+2$ is that it is *linear*. That is
what we want a notation for.
:::

## Asymptotics, reprised {.smaller}

$T(n) = O(f(n))$ if there are positive constants $c$ and $n_0$ such that

$$T(n) \le c \cdot f(n) \quad \text{for all } n \ge n_0$$

\

"Eventually, and up to a constant factor, $T$ is no worse than $f$."

::: notes
Both quantifiers are load-bearing. c lets you ignore the machine; n_0 lets you
ignore small inputs. Students who have seen this in 121 still tend to forget
that n_0 exists, which is what makes them argue about small cases.
:::

## The reminder page {.smaller}

::: {.shaded-table}

| growth | name | |
|---|---|---|
| $O(1)$ | constant | |
| $O(\log n)$ | logarithmic | |
| $O(\log^k n)$ | poly-log | |
| $O(n)$ | linear | |
| $O(n \log n)$ | log-linear | |
| $O(n^{1+c})$ | superlinear | $c > 0$ |
| $O(n^2)$ | quadratic | |
| $O(n^3)$ | cubic | |
| $O(n^k)$ | polynomial | "tractable" |
| $O(c^n)$ | exponential | "intractable" |

:::

::: notes
Point back at Friday's running-times table -- the tractable/intractable line
is exactly where $2^n$ ran past the age of the universe.
:::

## Runtime analysis guidelines {.smaller}

- Single operations — **constant** time
- Consecutive operations — **additive**
- Conditionals — constant for the test, plus the branch taken
- Loops — **sum of the loop body** times
- Function call — the time for that function

::: notes
These are the rules they will use on every homework this term. Nothing here is
surprising; the value is having them written down in one place.
:::

## Back to where we started {.smaller}

```cpp
int idxFirst (vector<int> arr, int q) {
    for (int i = 0; i < arr.size(); i++)
        if (arr[i] == q)
            return i;
    return -1;
}
```

In the worst case, $T(n) = $

\

Which should we use to describe it? &nbsp; $o \quad O \quad \omega \quad \Omega \quad \theta \quad \Theta$

::: notes
Worst case is $\Theta(n)$ -- and the interesting part is *why not O(n)*. O is
an upper bound and is true but weak: $O(n^2)$ is also a correct statement about
this function. Theta is the one that says what you actually mean.

This is the distinction that gets tested, and it is the one students most
reliably fudge.
:::
